paras: The shooting of David Kenney and manhunt for Charles Johnson took place at Gadsden, Alabama, on about November 12, 1888, when Officer Kenney was fatally shot while trying to make an arrest and some 150 men set out after the accused man. A wire dispatch predicted that Johnson would be lynched if caught, but no report of his capture or fate was found.

According to a Chattanooga dispatch dated November 13, Officers David Kenney and John Cunningham went to a house at Gadsden the day before "to arrest a negro." Charles Johnson, alias Holmes, was said to have shot Kenney in the breast, and Kenney died of the wound within three hours. This account of the shooting is the only one in the coverage, and it does not say why the officers sought the arrest.

By the time the dispatch was sent, 150 men were hunting Johnson, whom the wire called "the murderer." The dispatch added that he "will be lynched if caught," without saying whether the men were a sheriff's posse or acting on their own.
No report of Johnson's capture, lynching, escape or trial appears in the coverage, and no inquest into Kenney's death is reported.

The story reached readers outside Alabama only as a one-paragraph wire item. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer printed a condensed version among its "Telegraphic Taps" on November 13, spelling the town "Gadsen" and saying Johnson "shot and killed" Kenney. On November 14 the Richmond Daily Times ran the fuller text under "Brief Telegrams," and the Annapolis Evening Capital printed it under the headline "Murdered the Officer" with a November 14 dateline.

All three papers repeated the officers' account as fact and reported the expected lynching without comment. Johnson's race appeared only in the phrase "to arrest a negro," and Kenney's race was not stated.

All three articles reprint one Chattanooga wire dispatch with near-identical wording, so they are not independent reports (A1, A2, A3).

record_check.dossier: threatened: the coverage reports only a hunt and a prediction of lynching, no attempt on Johnson

Black, by inference: the officers went 'to arrest a negro' and Johnson is the man who shot
150 men hunting; the dispatch does not say they were a deputized posse
One officer (Kenney) killed by the accused; his race is not stated
1888-11-12, the 'yesterday' of a November 13 dispatch; November 14 is only a later dateline
